extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in mathematical logic and computability theory
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, theorems, and model descriptions governing recursive (total and partial) functions, their normal form and indexing, computability via register machines, reducibility, Rice's theorem, and formal provability predicates used in the incompleteness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: m-place partial function (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An m-place partial function is a function f with dom f ⊆ N^m and ran f ⊆ N. If a tuple a ∉ dom f then f(a) is said to be undefined; if dom f = N^m then f is total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary note: 'partial' and 'total' are not antonyms in ordinary language here; the phrase 'recursive partial function' is an indivisible technical phrase (a recursive partial function need not be recursive as a relation).

rubrics_metrics.name: computable partial function (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An m-place partial function f is computable iff there is an effective procedure such that (a) given an m-tuple a in dom f the procedure produces f(a); and (b) given an m-tuple a not in dom f the procedure produces no output at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This extends the earlier definition for total functions; the key behavioral requirement is that computations for inputs outside the domain must not produce output (i.e., they diverge).

rubrics_metrics.name: computability ↔ effective enumerability (Theorem 36C)
rubrics_metrics.description: An m-place partial function f is computable iff f (as an (m+1)-ary relation) is effectively enumerable (recursively enumerable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: from an enumeration of the relation, watch for tuples with the given prefix to output values; conversely, dovetail (interleave) computations of f on all inputs to enumerate its graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: recursive partial function (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recursive partial function is a partial function that, as a relation, is recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology note: 'recursive partial function' does not imply the relation is recursive — only recursively enumerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: recursive partial vs recursive for total functions (Theorem 36D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f: N^m → N is total, then f is a recursive partial function iff f is recursive (as a relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For total functions, the notions coincide because totality allows turning an r.e. graph into a decidable relation by pairing values; the proof uses characterization of complements and Theorem 35F.

rubrics_metrics.name: indexing / universal representation ([[e]]_m) (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each e ∈ N define the m-place partial function [[e]]_m(a1,...,am) = U(μk e, a1,...,am, k ∈ T_m), understood as undefined if no such k exists. The index e is the 'program' and [[e]]_m is the function with that index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a numbering (indexing) [[0]]_1, [[1]]_1, ... of all one-place recursive partial functions; U and T_m are recursive, so this is an effective encoding of programs and their outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Form Theorem (Kleene, 1943)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) The (m+1)-place partial function whose value at (e,a1,...,am) is [[e]]_m(a1,...,am) is a recursive partial function. (b) For each e ≥ 0, [[e]]_m is an m-place recursive partial function. (c) Any m-place recursive partial function equals [[e]]_m for some e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes universality: there is a universal partial function and every recursive partial function has an index. The theorem shows how representability in a formal system yields indices (Godel numbers) that act as 'programs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: undecidability of totality of indices (Theorem 36E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set { e | [[e]]_1 is total } is not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses diagonalization: construct a total function f that would lead to contradiction if this index-totality set were recursive; classification: this set is in Σ^0_2 but not recursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: K = { a | [[a]]_1(a) defined } is r.e. but not recursive (Theorem 36F)
rubrics_metrics.description: K is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via diagonal function g(a) = [[a]]_1(a) + 1 if a ∈ K, else 0; shows K cannot be recursive by the usual self-reference contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: unsolvability of the halting problem (Corollary 36G)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation { (e,a) | [[e]]_1(a) is defined } is not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently: there is no effective method that, given a program e and input a, decides whether the computation halts (is defined) on that input; reduces K to this relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: characterization of r.e. relations (Theorem 36H)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation on N is recursively enumerable iff it is the domain of some recursive partial function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: given r.e. relation Q expressible as ∃b R(a,b) with R recursive, define f(a) = μb R(a,b) which is recursive as a relation and has domain Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: parameter theorem / S-m-n theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For each m ≥ 1 and n ≥ 1 there is a recursive function ρ such that for any e, a (parameters), b (arguments): [[e]]_{m+n}(a1,...,am,b1,...,b_n) = [[ρ(e,a1,...,am)]]_n(b1,...,b_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: we can effectively 'plug in' parameters into a program to produce an index for the resulting specialized program. Proof given via normal form and representability; useful for effective transformations and many-one reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of parameter theorem for many-one reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The parameter theorem yields total recursive functions g that transform indices to produce desired behavior (e.g., to reduce membership in K to membership in another set A by producing indices whose domains/outputs encode [[a]]_1(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show { a | W_a = ∅ } is not recursive, construct g(a) with [[g(a)]]_1(b) = [[a]]_1(a) for all b so that dom[[g(a)]]_1 empty ⇔ [[a]]_1(a) undefined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rice's theorem (Theorem 36J)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C be a set of one-place recursive partial functions. Then the set IC = { e | [[e]]_1 ∈ C } of indices of members of C is recursive iff either C is empty or C contains all one-place recursive partial functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nontrivial semantic properties of computable functions are undecidable (index sets are nonrecursive) — proof by reduction from K using parameter theorem to construct indices with prescribed behavior depending on membership in K.

rubrics_metrics.name: register machine instruction semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: A register machine has finitely many registers 1..K storing natural numbers. Program instructions are: I r (increment r: add 1, then proceed to next instruction); D r (decrement r: if register nonzero, subtract 1 and skip next instruction, else proceed to next instruction); T q (transfer q: move control q instructions relative to this one; halt if target instruction doesn't exist; T0 loops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These instructions define a simple idealized computing model equivalent in power to other models (Turing, etc.). Examples given: clearing a register, moving numbers, addition program, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: program calculates f (definition for register machines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an n-place partial function f, a program P calculates f iff: (i) if f(a1,...,an) is defined then the machine started with a1..an in registers 1..n eventually halts seeking instruction p+1 (p length of P) with f(a1,..,an) in register n+1; (ii) if f(a1,...,an) is undefined then the calculation never terminates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures the intended operational behavior on inputs — halting with output iff the function is defined, divergence otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: equivalence: register-machine computability = recursive partial (Theorem 36K)
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial function f is calculable by some register-machine program iff f is a recursive partial function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: arithmetize calculations to show register-machine computable functions are r.e.; conversely show primitive recursive building blocks and closure under composition/μ yield implementability by register machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: provability predicate Prb_T (definition) and numeralwise representation
rubrics_metrics.description: For a recursively axiomatizable theory T with recursive axioms A, fix a recursive relation π(v1,v2) that numeralwise represents 'v2 is a deduction number from A whose last component is the sentence coded by v1.' Define Prb_T(σ) = ∃v2 π(S(σ)0, v2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: (a) if T ⊢ σ then AE ⊢ Prb_T(σ); (b) if T includes AE then T has reflection: T ⊢ σ ⇒ T ⊢ Prb_T(σ).

rubrics_metrics.name: sufficiently strong theory (three derivability conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Call T sufficiently strong if: (1) AE ⊆ T (so T has reflection property); (2) For any σ, T ⊢ (Prb_T(σ) → Prb_T(Prb_T(σ))); (3) For any ρ, σ, T ⊢ (Prb_T(ρ → σ) → (Prb_T(ρ) → Prb_T(σ))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formalized derivability conditions are the technical hypotheses used to carry out the second incompleteness argument inside T; they formalize that T can reason about its own provability predicate with basic properties of provability and modus ponens.

rubrics_metrics.name: formalized intermediate lemma used in second incompleteness (Formalized Lemma 37B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume T is sufficiently strong and recursively axiomatizable. If σ is a sentence with AE ⊢ (σ ↔ ¬ Prb_T(σ)), then T ⊢ (Cons_T → ¬ Prb_T(σ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is a formalized version of the standard incompleteness step: within T, consistency implies that the fixed-point sentence asserting its own unprovability is indeed unprovable; assembling the remaining derivability steps yields the usual second-incompleteness conclusion.
